title: Segregation on the road and the white trumpeter at the filling station
summary: Prompted by Earl Warren's stories, he tells how a white trumpet player in his band was sent to the colored restroom at a southern gas station.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, Earl Warren. In fact, Earl
Warren, he could really tell you some good stories. I know he's told you some.
: When he was in the South and they all had to stay in terrible places. He'd walk into a good hotel and make them mad.

And then a lot of times, he'd probably have to go get food for them. You know? And it's funny, but it's true. I had a white fella that was playing with me. We were down South one time. And I think it was going through either Georgia or Alabama and we stopped to get gas and that's when they had colored restrooms and they had white restrooms. So, you know, quite naturally, him being with the band, you know, he -- we stopped to pull in there and he just went on to the restroom. Well, it was this white restroom. Well, he come out. The fella happened to see him come out. He didn't know that he went in there, the filling station attendant, and he come back, say, "Say, boy don't you know that's a white restroom?" So I winked at the -- he was a trumpet player -- I winked at him, so then he says, "No, I'm sorry. I thought that was the restroom and I just went to the restroom and I didn't think." He says, "Let me get you straight right now." And he went around and showed him where the colored restroom was and the guy was just as white. He was white, you know, and I just kept winking at him until -- you know. Then he

told him he was sorry and then the guy got so mad at the station, he wanted to fight him, you know. So I says, "Oh no, everything's all right. I'll get him out of here. I'll take care of him." So we got on out of there, you know. And it was just something like that and the guy was white, but he figured that he had to be colored because he was with us.
And he probably would have made trouble if he'd known he was anyway.
Well, that's true. You know what I mean.
So, it's like you say, six and a half a dozen.
